headline: DRS barcode countdown, a construction-product data library and CBAM verification rules all move this week
executive_summary: This first live week of the Regulatory Radar is quieter than the seeded sample, but the items that did land are operational rather than rhetorical. GS1 UK used 9 September to tell members that the one-year DRS countdown starts on 1 October 2026 and that barcode change, Scheme Article List registration and stock planning must now sit inside a single implementation programme. On 10 September MHCLG's Grenfell progress report confirmed that government responses to the Construction Products Reform White Paper and General Safety Requirement consultations will come later this year, with GSR legislation to follow when parliamentary time allows, and that a digital discovery for a construction-product information library is under way this quarter. HMRC laid the CBAM Emissions and Verification Regulations on 9 September, locking in how embodied-emissions data for aluminium, cement, fertiliser, hydrogen, iron and steel must be monitored and independently verified from 1 January 2027. In healthcare, DHSC published the Health Bill medical-device licensing impact assessment and fact sheet: the Bill itself creates no new UDI or labelling duty, but it does give MHRA the power to build a GB licensing route that will have to sit alongside the still-pending 2026 UDI regulations. For GS1 UK the practical task this week is to get drinks members allocating GTINs now, to put identifier and data-carrier language in front of MHCLG's digital-library discovery, and to keep the GB UDI designation question on MHRA's desk.
cross_sector_themes: Regulators are moving from consultation to implementation mechanics: DRS Article List barcodes, a construction-product data library, and verified CBAM emissions records
Unique identification is being specified as a scheme or tax data key (DRS GTIN/barcode; CBAM commodity-code goods) rather than as a named GS1 legal mandate
2027 remains the crunch year: DRS go-live 1 October, CBAM charge from 1 January, construction GSR still aimed at late 2027, GB UDI still planned for mid-2027
A live UK digital product record call for evidence closes on 21 September 2026 – the last chance this month to argue for a single data carrier interoperable with the EU DPP

sector_overviews.headline: DRS leaves the awareness phase: barcode change and retailer readiness are now a 12-month programme
sector_overviews.summary: GS1 UK's 9 September briefing is the clearest retail signal this week. With Exchange for Change already appointed across the four nations, intended producer fees published (0p from October 2027 to December 2028) and a monthly retailer readiness survey launched on 7 September, members no longer have an excuse to treat DRS as a 2027 artwork job. Existing barcodes on in-scope PET, steel and aluminium containers (and glass in Wales) still need to change and be registered on the Scheme Article List; RVMs must read EAN/UPC and 2D codes. Separately, HMRC laid the CBAM emissions-and-verification rules that importers of iron, steel, aluminium, cement, fertiliser and hydrogen will use from 1 January 2027. Nothing new landed this week on packaging EPR labelling, Windsor Framework 'Not for EU' marks, Sunrise 2027 POS readiness or the April 2029 e-invoicing mandate.

sector_overviews.headline: Government will answer the GSR consultation later this year and is already designing a digital product library
sector_overviews.summary: The 10 September Grenfell Tower Inquiry progress report is this week's construction event. MHCLG says it is considering the White Paper and GSR consultation responses (closed May 2026) and intends to publish government responses later in 2026, then bring forward GSR legislation when parliamentary time allows. That keeps the late-2027 commencement window in play but slips the 'regulations by end-2026' ambition onto a parliamentary-time caveat. More immediately for GS1 UK, recommendation 24 records that an expert digital consultancy has been commissioned to run a digital discovery in Q3 2026 for a construction-product information library, with Alpha testing of viable solutions to follow. That is the live design conversation in which unique identifiers, QR/GS1 Digital Link data carriers and GDSN-style product records need to be tabled. No new SI on construction products, UKCA/CE or PAS 2000 was laid this week.

sector_overviews.headline: Health Bill papers give MHRA a future licensing power; statutory GB UDI is still the December 2026 instrument to watch
sector_overviews.summary: Healthcare had no new UDI, Scan4Safety or MDOR instrument this week. What did appear, on 9 September, is the Health Bill package on medicines and medical-devices regulatory reform: a fact sheet plus a final-stage impact assessment on a future MHRA device-licensing regime. The Bill, introduced in May, would let the Secretary of State establish through later regulations a route in which MHRA can assess and licence devices (and certain manufacturers, importers and wholesalers) directly, including with conditions. DHSC is explicit that the Bill itself creates no new requirements for manufacturers or providers. That still matters to GS1 UK because any GB licensing database will need to key devices consistently with the draft Medical Devices (Amendment) Regulations 2026, which would make UDI compulsory from mid-2027. The NHS Supply Chain Scan4Safety IMS framework (live since June 2026) and the New Hospitals Programme 2027 GS1 requirement were not updated this week.

items.title: GS1 UK: one-year DRS countdown starts 1 October 2026 – barcodes must change and be registered
items.summary: On 9 September 2026 GS1 UK told members that 1 October 2026 is the one-year mark before the UK deposit return scheme goes live. Exchange for Change is the operator across all four nations, intended producer fees have been published, a monthly retailer readiness survey is running, and existing barcodes on in-scope containers still need to change and be registered on the Scheme Article List.
items.what_changed: GS1 UK published a DRS readiness briefing on 9 September 2026. It records that Exchange for Change has been appointed to operate the scheme across England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland; that intended producer fees will be 0p per container from October 2027 to December 2028, then (on current data) 0.6p for aluminium and steel and 2.3p for PET from January 2029, to be reconfirmed in May 2027; and that Exchange for Change has launched a monthly anonymous Retailer Readiness Survey (covered by Retail Gazette on 7 September). Reverse-vending-machine testing is under way, with a first certified-model list expected in early October 2026. GS1 UK restates Exchange for Change's material specification: every in-scope container must carry a barcode registered on the Scheme Article List; existing and many international barcodes must change; permitted carriers are EAN-13, EAN-8, UPC-A and UPC-E, compliant with the GS1 General Specifications or equivalent; and RVMs must also read 2D Data Matrix and QR codes. New DRS-specific barcodes and the scheme logo must not appear on packs sold to consumers before 1 October 2027. Scope remains PET, steel and aluminium 150 ml–3 L, with glass also in Wales.
items.why_it_matters_to_gs1: This is the core GS1 UK retail programme for the next 12 months. The scheme does not invent a new identifier: it requires a unique, GS1-spec barcode on every in-scope container, registered on an identifier-keyed Article List that RVMs and counting centres will poll. That is GTIN allocation, barcode quality, artwork, productDNA/GDSN attribute updates and stock-run-out planning under another name. Members who treat it as a late 2027 print job will miss production lead times and will have unregistered stock that RVMs reject. International GTINs used on multi-market SKUs may attract an extra producer-fee charge if they are not DRS-specific; GS1 UK should keep pressing Exchange for Change for a published rule and for 2D / GS1 Digital Link to be a first-class return code, not only a secondary RVM capability. If members do nothing, they risk unsaleable in-scope stock from 1 October 2027 and a scramble for new Company Prefix capacity.
gs1_standards_implicated: GS1 DataMatrix / QR codes powered by GS1 (RVM 2D read)
affected_stakeholders: Drinks producers, importers and own-label retailers
Grocery and convenience retailers operating return points

items.title: Grenfell progress report: GSR response later this year; digital product library discovery is live
items.issuing_body: Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG)
items.summary: On 10 September 2026 MHCLG published the latest Grenfell Tower Inquiry Phase 2 progress report. It confirms that government responses to the Construction Products Reform White Paper and General Safety Requirement consultations will come later this year, that GSR legislation will follow when parliamentary time allows, and that a digital discovery for a construction-product information library is being delivered this quarter.
items.what_changed: MHCLG published 'Progress report September 2026: the construction industry' on 10 September 2026 as part of the Grenfell Tower Inquiry government progress report. On recommendations 13 and 14 (conformity assessment and test-data transparency) the department says the White Paper and GSR consultations closed in May, responses are being considered with industry and regulators, government responses will be published later in the year, and next steps include bringing forward legislation to introduce a General Safety Requirement when parliamentary time allows. On recommendation 24 (a digitally based library of product and fire-performance information) MHCLG repeats that intent and adds a new delivery fact: an expert digital consultancy has been commissioned to deliver a digital discovery in Q3 (July to September) 2026, followed by Alpha testing of viable solutions. Separately, the Building Safety Regulator's Approved Document B consultation closed on 1 July 2026 with more than 500 responses; recommendations are now expected by March 2027. The Building Safety Regulator's transfer out of HSE into an MHCLG-sponsored arm's-length body was completed in June 2026 and is treated as a step towards a single construction regulator.
items.why_it_matters_to_gs1: The White Paper and GSR consultation already proposed unique identifiers, scannable (including QR) data carriers and digital product records for construction products. This week's report does not restate those design choices, but it does two things GS1 UK needed: it keeps GSR legislation on the 2026/27 track, and it opens a live digital-discovery / Alpha for the product-information library that will have to key records somehow. If that library is built on proprietary or document-centric IDs, manufacturers will run a parallel numbering scheme on top of GTINs they already use for merchants and, for exporters, the EU DPP. GS1 UK should treat Q3 2026 discovery as a now conversation: GTIN (and GMN where a model-level key is needed), GS1 Digital Link as the QR on the product, and a GDSN/productDNA-compatible attribute set feeding both the golden thread and any future UK digital product record. If members do nothing, they will be asked for digital product data in 2027 without allocated identifiers or a resolver.
gs1_standards_implicated: GS1 Digital Link / QR codes powered by GS1
affected_stakeholders: Dutyholders under the Building Safety Act / golden thread
OPSS as national regulator for construction products

items.title: CBAM Emissions and Verification Regulations 2026 laid – verified product emissions data from 1 January 2027
items.summary: The Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (Emissions and Verification) Regulations 2026 were made on 8 September and laid on 9 September. From 1 January 2027, importers of aluminium, cement, fertiliser, hydrogen, iron and steel must support CBAM returns with monitored, independently verified emissions data (or default values) for each type of CBAM good.
items.what_changed: HMRC and the Treasury laid SI 2026/995 on 9 September 2026 (made 8 September; in force 1 January 2027). The instrument sets how embodied emissions in a CBAM good are calculated, how operators must monitor relevant emissions over a calendar-year monitoring period, and how an independent accredited verifier must produce a verification report and opinion statement. Record-keeping duties apply to registered importers who submit verified emissions intensity on a return. HMRC updated the CBAM policy summary the same day to record the laying, and updated the November 2025 tax information and impact note with revised one-off and ongoing cost estimates. CBAM itself was created by the Finance Act 2026 and applies from 1 January 2027 to goods in aluminium, cement, fertiliser, hydrogen, and iron and steel. Goods are typed by commodity code in Schedule 16 to the Finance Act 2026, not by a named unique product identifier. Earlier administrative, rate-calculation and transitory SIs were laid on 13 July 2026.
items.why_it_matters_to_gs1: CBAM is a carbon tax keyed on commodity code, weight and verified emissions intensity, not a barcode mandate. It still passes the relevance test because it forces structured, regulator-facing product data down the metals, cement, fertiliser and hydrogen chains that supply UK retail packaging, construction products and (for hydrogen) energy-intensive manufacturing. Importers will need a durable link from a customs line to a production installation, a precursor-goods bill of materials and a six-year evidence pack. GLN for the installation and legal entity, GTIN or GIAI where the same article is also traded as a merchanted product, and EPCIS-style process events are ways members can meet that data duty interoperably; the SI does not require them. Construction-product manufacturers using imported steel, aluminium or cement will feel this as a cost-and-data problem on top of GSR/DPP. If members do nothing they can still file using default values, but they will overpay and will not have the master data that EU CBAM and, later, DPP/EUDR also demand.
gs1_standards_implicated: GTIN (where the CBAM good is also a traded article)
GDSN attributes for origin and composition
affected_stakeholders: UK importers of iron, steel, aluminium, cement, fertiliser and hydrogen

items.title: Health Bill fact sheet: powers for a future MHRA medical-device licensing regime
items.issuing_body: Department of Health and Social Care / MHRA
items.summary: On 9 September 2026 DHSC published a Health Bill fact sheet and a final-stage impact assessment on a future medical-device licensing regime. The Bill would let MHRA assess and licence devices directly through later regulations. It does not itself impose UDI, implant cards or new labelling duties.
items.what_changed: DHSC added several Health Bill supporting documents on 9 September 2026, including 'Health Bill: medicines and medical devices regulatory reforms – fact sheet' and 'Health Bill: medical device licensing regime – impact assessment' (DHSCIA9724, dated 22 June 2026, published 9 September). The Bill, introduced in the Commons on 14 May 2026, would (1) make it easier to update medicines and devices law (ambulatory references, proportionate consultation, negative procedure for minor/technical changes), (2) give MHRA clearer powers to share selected medicines and devices information with UK and international partners, and (3) confer powers under the Medicines and Medical Devices Act 2021 to establish, by subsequent secondary legislation, a medical-device licensing regime. Under that future model MHRA could directly assess and licence devices and certain manufacturers, importers and wholesalers, including with conditions. The fact sheet is explicit that the Bill does not itself establish the regime and creates no new requirements for manufacturers, healthcare providers or patients. Today's GB routes remain UKCA (via UK Approved Bodies for medium/high risk) and time-limited CE recognition. The impact assessment notes MHRA has consulted on indefinite CE recognition and records 61,000–100,000 UKCA device registrations since 2025.
items.why_it_matters_to_gs1: This is not a UDI instrument and must not be reported as one. It still matters because any MHRA licence register will become another identifier-keyed database sitting next to device registration, MDOR and the draft December 2026 UDI regulations. If those systems use different device keys, Scan4Safety trusts will scan a GS1 GTIN/UDI-DI that the licensing database cannot match. GS1 UK's interest is to have DHSC/MHRA say, when they consult on the secondary legislation, that a licence record should carry the same UDI-DI (GTIN) and Basic UDI-DI (GMN) that the draft 2026 amendment regulations would make compulsory. Information-sharing powers also make it more likely that licence, registration and vigilance data will move between MHRA, NICE and the NHS – all of which already lean on GS1 keys in Scan4Safety and NHS eProcurement. If members do nothing they should still prepare for UDI; they do not need to redesign labels for this Bill.
affected_stakeholders: Medical device and IVD manufacturers and UK Responsible Persons
